source.title: Chemical reasoning in LLMs unlocks steerable synthesis planning and reaction mechanism elucidation
source.authors: Andrés M Bran; Théo A. Neukomm; Daniel P. Armstrong; Zlatko Joncev; P. Schwaller

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary information are present. Some references to supplementary material appear as “SI-??”, but this does not prevent reading the reported results.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates chemical-task performance across language models and explicitly reports a relationship with model size, but does not measure pretraining loss or reproduce the original scaling-law analyses.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and makes general statements about scaling in its supplementary information, but does not test held-out cross-entropy, parameter/token/compute power laws, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. The chemistry benchmark results below are the relevant reported evidence for downstream task performance; the study gives no parameter counts or fitted performance-versus-size curve.
record.test_reason: An applied chemistry paper that benchmarks commercial and open LLMs as evaluators inside a search framework. It measures no pretraining loss and reports no parameter counts, compute or fitted curve. The models differ in provider, generation, post-training and reasoning training, so size is not isolated. Its remark that 'performance scales strongly with model size' is a qualitative aside, and the authors frame it as a threshold or emergence effect rather than predictable improvement. That cannot show whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale, so no version is tested. Kaplan et al. is cited only as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that LLMs used as evaluators within search can perform strategy-aware synthesis planning and mechanism elucidation. They say newer and larger models reason better, and frame the size effect as an emergence threshold, not smooth scaling. Smaller models are near random even on short routes, and long routes defeat all models except Gemini-2.5-pro.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates chemistry-task performance across LLMs; it does not use the original scaling-law measurement or fitting procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance depends on task difficulty and model choice; the authors report a distinct limitation on long synthetic routes.

fits_no_version.finding: Across commercial and open LLMs of undisclosed size, smaller or distilled models score near random on chemistry route-alignment and mechanism tasks. Examples: GPT-4o-mini top-1 of 5–50% vs GPT-4o 18–70% (Table 1, random 17%); DeepSeek-r1 distills and o4-mini trail their larger counterparts. The authors frame this as a capability threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Specialised chemical-reasoning benchmark performance appears only above an (unquantified) model-capability threshold, confounded with model generation and post-training.

record.problems: No parameter counts or quantitative performance-versus-size fit are reported for the scale comparison. The long-route result is qualitative in the main text.
record.rows_left_out: The paper also reports detailed per-model mechanism-elucidation accuracies and additional strategy-planning benchmark results. They are not extracted as separate rows because the study does not report those results as a controlled or quantified scale analysis; the cited aggregate scale comparison and its stated long-route limitation are retained.

untested.parts: All: no scaling in other modalities or regimes.
Predictable downstream improvement with parameters, compute or loss. Sizes are unknown and confounded with post-training; only a qualitative 'larger/newer is better' remark is made.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 'supports' label should be dropped. The size claim gives no parameter counts and mixes providers, generations and reasoning-trained models; the SI 'Evolution of capability' plot is over release date, not scale. Only within-family pairs (4o-mini vs 4o, DeepSeek-r1 vs distills, Llama sizes in SI Fig 4c, values unreadable) touch on size, and these are distillation-confounded.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions and power-law ranges.
Prediction of larger-run loss from fits to smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior across other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
No pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance analysis, quantitative scaling curve, or parameter counts; the reported comparisons are chemistry tasks across different models.
The study does not compare scaling-law fits or their setup and fitting choices.

rows.subject: LLMs evaluated on the strategy-aware synthesis-planning benchmark (aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: Different model sizes; parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared model performance on a benchmark of route-to-prompt alignment.

conditions.value: Different sizes; individual sizes not stated

rows.measure: Correlation between model-produced scores and benchmark ground-truth scores.
rows.value: Performance scales strongly with model size; smaller models’ performance is indistinguishable from random choice even for short routes. Gemini-2.5-pro achieves the highest scores.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this qualitative comparison
rows.locator: Section 2.1; Figure 2a and supplementary extended benchmarking results
rows.note: Aggregate qualitative result reported by the authors; no numerical parameter counts or fitted scale-performance relationship are provided.
rows.check: Models of undisclosed size from different providers and generations, confounded with post-training and reasoning training. No sizes, no curve, and the claim rests on unreadable SI figures. It cannot show predictable scaling; it is a qualitative cross-model comparison. State 'partial' is unsupported.

rows.subject: LLMs evaluated on the strategy-aware synthesis-planning benchmark (aggregate comparison)
rows.size_stated: Different models; parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated route-alignment scores on the most complex targets.
rows.measure: Ability to distinguish and select routes aligned with the prompt; exact value not stated in text.
rows.value: All models struggle, except Gemini-2.5-pro; the authors also report positive correlations in these extreme cases.
rows.note: Reported as an aggregate comparison; the text does not provide numerical scores for this condition.
rows.check: About task difficulty (long routes, Target 4) and one model (Gemini-2.5-pro) being best. It involves no scale variable, so it bears on no version. No numeric value is given.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Strategy-aware synthesis-planning benchmark, aggregate model-size comparison
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that performance rises strongly with model size and that smaller models are at random-choice performance (r1). This is qualitative evidence on a chemistry task, not a fitted or quantitative scaling relationship.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Most complex synthesis-planning target, routes up to 50 reactions
reader_labels.reason: Performance is incomplete on long routes: all models struggle apart from Gemini-2.5-pro (r2).
